newsitem.title: UK: Russian fuel export pattern puzzles West's traders.
newsitem.headline: Russian fuel export pattern puzzles West's traders.

text.p: Russia has poured out much more cracked fuel than expected in the first part its summer export programme, puzzling Western traders who had anticipated a healthy flow of high value straight-run fuel.

The abundance of cracked fuel at the start of the traditional summer export flood has depressed the Rotterdam barge market and led to a scramble for what little good quality straight-run fuel has been on offer, traders said.
"We are certainly a little over-balanced on the cracked side," said one specialist seller of Russian fuel. "I would estimate it's about 60 to 40, cracked to straight-run."
"I would agree that there is more cracked fuel this year than last (in north-west Europe) but then last year was very bad," he added on Friday.
Although traders were unable to pinpoint exactly the relative quantities of material on offer the effect on prices has already been marked.

Even during crude's recent rally barge prices in the Rotterdam area failed to rise because of the depressing effects of Russian exports, and values are now on the verge of plunging below the $80 mark to fresh two-year lows.

Meanwhile, good quality Russian E-4 straight-runs are attracting premiums of five to six dollars above the three means pricing formula and M100s were heard offered mid-week at a healthy seven dollars above the two means.
The Mediterranean bunker market has also seen good supplies of both cracked and straight-run fuel from the Black Sea.
Although the effect on prices has been marked, the causes of the unusual export pattern are disputed.
Minor refining upgrades, different marketing patterns and logistical problems have all contributed, with no one factor predominating, Russian export experts say.

"With the current high internal prices for crude and rather low product prices in Europe only the really big companies can keep refineries going to export," said Stanislav Gorbunov of Finnish-based exporter Crudex Oil.
"The export slate of the larger companies is more geared to cracked fuel," he said, with smaller refineries running at low capacity and selling their straight-run locally.

Inland refineries which have cat-crackers are now free to export since canals have de-iced, Gorbunov added, with the blending necessitated by the long transport chain also tending to put most product in the cracked category.

The three YUKOS refineries were mixing their production for export to produce semi-straight fuel that western refineries price at cracked value because they cannot put it into sophisticated upgrading equipment, said Gorbunov.
Western traders agreed that some material was contaminated in transit, with strands of cracked fuel reducing the value of the straight-run it is mixed with.
Selling behaviour has also changed the market.
"A lot more E4s are going under term contracts this year than before," said one refinery fuel buyer, "which is why so little is offered spot and premiums have been driven up."

Most analysts believe Russian refineries are antiquated, inefficient and in need of millions of dollars of investment before they can maximise yields, but some traders think there have been modest improvements in refinery engineering.

"I think they have been tuning up their systems to squeeze the barrel more," said one trader. "They have closed the gaps and cut leaks and losses to get more yield by producing more gas oil and less straight-run."
